title: How The Biohazard Sign Was Born
sources: 99% Invisible, 'Biohazard: Iconic Symbol Designed to be Memorable but Meaningless' (Charles Baldwin, environmental-health engineer at Dow Chemical, 1966; design goal 'memorable but meaningless')
Wikipedia, 'Biological hazard' (Baldwin of Dow Chemical with Robert S. Runkle of the NIH; paper in Science calling for a universal biological hazard symbol)

GIGAZINE, 'How was the biohazard's mark designed?' (six finalist designs; two-phase test scoring memorability, with meaninglessness as the tiebreak; winner highest on memorability, lowest on meaningfulness)
Auburn University, 'The Biohazard Symbol' (history of the design and its selection)
Print Magazine, 'The Daily Heller: An Existential Bio Logo' (Baldwin's account of choosing a mark with no known meaning that was easy to remember)

NOTE: sources conflict on the exact test sample (often quoted as 300 people in 25 cities, single-source) and on the Science publication date (1966 vs 13 October 1967). The narration stays vague on both and makes no claim about OSHA or ISO adoption.

lines.text: Before nineteen sixty-six, a lab full of deadly germs
might warn you with almost anything.
A skull, a cartoon bug, or nothing at all.
So Dow Chemical put an engineer named Charles Baldwin on it,
and he wanted a mark nobody had ever seen before.
then showed them to hundreds of people across dozens of cities,
asking a strange pair of questions:
which one do you remember, and which one means nothing to you?
The winner scored highest on memory and lowest on meaning.
That was the whole point: no story, no nation, no animal,
so every lab on Earth could be taught the same thing.
